title: The LORD Looks on the Heart: David Anointed
summary: God sends the grieving Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint one of Jesse's sons as king. Samuel is impressed by the tall eldest son, but the LORD tells him that he does not see as people see: he looks on the heart. The youngest, David, is called in from the sheep and anointed, and the Spirit of the LORD rushes upon him. Meanwhile the Spirit leaves Saul, a tormenting spirit troubles him, and David is brought to court to play the harp and becomes Saul's armor-bearer.
story: Chapter 15 ended with Samuel mourning Saul and the LORD regretting that he had made him king. Chapter 16 opens a new movement in the books of Samuel, the rise of David, which runs through the rest of 1 Samuel and into 2 Samuel 5, where David is finally king over all Israel. The chapter makes two moves that the rest of the story unfolds. First, God privately chooses and anoints David, so that everything that follows (the giant, the jealousy, the years as a fugitive) is the working out of a choice already made. Second, God brings David into Saul's own household, so the rejected king and the chosen king now live side by side. The man “after His own heart” promised in 13:14 finally has a name.
historical:
Bethlehem was a small town in the hill country of Judah, about six miles south of later Jerusalem. It was the setting of the story of Ruth, and Ruth 4:17-22 traces David's line through Boaz and Ruth to Obed, Jesse, and David. David's reign is usually dated to roughly 1010 to 970 BC, so this anointing takes place some years before, while Saul still reigns. How many years is not stated; David is still young enough to be tending sheep.

Samuel's fear that Saul would kill him (verse 2) shows how far relations had broken down. Anointing another king while the reigning king lived was an act of treason in any ancient kingdom. The elders of Bethlehem, trembling at the prophet's arrival (verse 4), may simply have feared that a visit from such a figure meant judgment, or they may already have sensed the danger of being caught between Samuel and the king. The text does not say which. The list of Jesse's sons here and in 17:12 implies eight sons, while 1 Chronicles 2:13-15 names seven, with David as the seventh; the difference has been explained in several ways, and the text does not settle it.
cultural:
Anointing with oil marked a person as set apart for a task by God. Priests were anointed (Exodus 29:7), and so were kings; the oil was poured on the head from a horn or flask. Samuel's sacrifice at Bethlehem was a real act of worship, and it provided a public occasion for the family gathering. To consecrate the guests meant to have them prepare ritually, by washing and avoiding what made them unclean, before sharing in a sacrificial meal. Refusing to sit down to eat until David arrived shows how central he has become: the feast waits for the youngest.

In a society where the firstborn son held priority, the choice of the youngest was a deliberate reversal, and it repeats a pattern already seen in Genesis (Abel, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph). Tending sheep was the ordinary work given to younger sons and servants. The harp in verse 16 translates a word (kinnor) for a small stringed instrument, more like a lyre than a modern harp. Music was widely believed to calm troubled minds, and court musicians appear in many ancient cultures. The gifts Jesse sends to Saul (bread, wine, a young goat) were the customary courtesy when a son entered a greater man's service.
literary: The chapter has two panels. In the first (verses 1 to 13) the LORD speaks, Samuel sees, and the key word is sight: Samuel “saw” Eliab, the LORD tells him not to consider appearance, and the LORD “sees the heart.” The sons pass before Samuel in a slow, repetitive procession, which builds suspense before the unnamed youngest is called. David's name is withheld until the Spirit rushes upon him in verse 13, which makes his naming coincide with his anointing. In the second panel (verses 14 to 23) Saul's servants speak, and the pattern reverses: the Spirit leaves Saul and a spirit of distress comes. The two halves are linked by the phrase “the Spirit of the LORD,” coming upon David and departing from Saul in consecutive verses.

outline.t: The LORD sends Samuel to Bethlehem
David anointed and the Spirit rushes upon him
The Spirit leaves Saul; a musician is sought

doctrines.note: God has “selected” a king for himself and guides Samuel step by step. The choice of the least likely son shows that God's purposes do not depend on human rank or expectation.

The Spirit of the LORD comes upon David to equip him for his calling, and departs from Saul. In the Old Testament the Spirit often empowers particular people for particular tasks; here the transfer of the Spirit marks the real transfer of kingship before the public one.
“Man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.” The value and calling of a person are not measured by stature, age, or impression. God knows people from the inside.

words.note: Mashach, to anoint. From this verb comes mashiach, anointed one, the word behind Messiah. David's anointing makes him the LORD's anointed, a title that later carries the hope of a coming son of David.

Tsalach, to rush. The Spirit “rushed” upon David, the same forceful verb used when the Spirit came on Samson (Judges 14:6) and Saul (10:6, 11:6). The difference is that for David it is “from that day forward,” a lasting presence rather than a burst of power for one battle.

Levav, heart, the inner self where thinking, choosing, and loyalty happen. The LORD sees this, not the outward appearance. The contrast answers the question raised in 13:14 about a man after God's own heart.

Ra, bad or harmful. The spirit that torments Saul is called a spirit of distress, or literally a bad or evil spirit. The word covers moral evil and also harm or misfortune, which is why translations vary between evil spirit and harmful spirit.

christ: Bethlehem, the town of Jesse and David, becomes the place where the Messiah is expected to be born (Micah 5:2), and Matthew and Luke both record Jesus' birth there. The prophets speak of a shoot from the stump of Jesse on whom the Spirit of the LORD will rest (Isaiah 11:1-2), language that echoes this chapter's anointing and the Spirit's coming. At Jesus' baptism the Spirit descends on him, marking him as the anointed Son, and the Gospels call him the son of David. David, the overlooked youngest son who was chosen and anointed but not yet enthroned, also sets a pattern that the story of Jesus fulfills in a deeper way: the true King is hidden in humility before he is revealed.

hard.q: What does it mean that “a spirit of distress from the LORD” tormented Saul? Does God send evil spirits?
hard.a: The text plainly says the spirit came from the LORD, and readers have understood it in several ways. Many see it as an evil spirit that God permitted or directed as judgment, in line with other passages where God uses hostile powers for his purposes (Judges 9:23; 1 Kings 22:19-23), without being the author of evil himself. Others emphasize that the Hebrew word can mean harmful or troubling rather than morally evil, and understand it as a divinely sent affliction of mind and spirit, while still treating it as God's judgment. The text does not name a condition, and it is wise not to diagnose one across three thousand years. Some readers combine both ideas. The Old Testament often traces all events, including disasters, back to God's sovereign rule without drawing the distinctions later theology would make. What the text insists on is that Saul's torment follows the Spirit's departure, and that even here God provides relief through David's music.

questions: Samuel was sure Eliab was the one. What outward qualities do you tend to trust when you judge people, and what might you be missing?
David was anointed and then sent back to the sheep and later to serve Saul. How do you live when God's calling seems far from being fulfilled?
Saul was helped by the very person who would replace him. What does that suggest about how God works in the lives of those who oppose his purposes?
